prompt:
# Write one principle card

You are writing a **principle card**: one mechanism, stated so precisely that
somebody who has never seen your sources could implement it and somebody else
could prove it wrong.

The card is not the implementation. A later step turns it into a behaviour-tree
leaf, and that step will be given **your card and nothing else** — not this
prompt, not your reasoning, not whatever you were given below. So everything the
implementer needs has to survive inside the six fields.

## The system the principle has to fit

A Unitree Go2 quadruped navigating an indoor space it has no map of. Below the
behaviour tree sits an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy: the
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`, saturated
to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and `|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Nothing you write touches the
policy, the gait or the joints.

What the robot can sense, once per control step:

```
t                    sim seconds since the episode started
ranges               181 lidar beams over a full circle, metres, inf where no return
range_angles         beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
range_max            6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
pose_estimate        (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, never ground truth
pose_error_estimate  scalar metres — how wrong we believe that belief is
contact              bool — are we touching something right now
goal                 (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of those are traps. `pose_estimate` **drifts** on some scenarios — a seeded
random walk is added to it — and ground truth is never observable. `goal` may be
`None`, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still scored against it but
this robot has not found it yet; it latches once seen.

## The task family this principle has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK BEGIN ---- -->
## What to base the principle on

The full text of a published paper is reproduced below. Read it and extract the
principle it establishes.

```
[PAPER TEXT REDACTED FROM THIS TRANSCRIPT — 73099 characters, sha256(pdf)=ff51f04ec7e6c174, extractor=cache. The corpus is an input and is never committed (out/corpus/ is gitignored). The prompt_hash recorded beside this is the hash of the REAL prompt, so a machine holding the PDF re-renders it byte-identically and replay finds this transcript.]
```

Work from the document, not from your memory of it. Where the two disagree, the
document wins. Quote its own threshold, exponent or closed form where it states
one, and put the section, page or equation number in `span` so somebody else can
check it.

The paper was written about something other than a quadruped with a planar
lidar. Carrying it across is the `derivation` field's whole job: say what in the
original maps onto what here, and say plainly where the mapping is yours rather
than the paper's.
<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK END ---- -->

## What a card is

Six fields. `mechanism`, `trigger` and `derivation` are prose. `prediction` is
**structured**, because a prediction that cannot be decided automatically cannot
become a unit test — and this one will be run as one, with no human in the loop.

```yaml
id: <short_snake_case_identifier>
node_name: <TheLeafThisWouldProduce>       # CamelCase, verb-first

source:
  citation: <the reference this principle comes from, or the single line
             "(no source - the principle was devised, not extracted)" if it
             comes from none>
  span: <the section, page, figure or equation number where the mechanism is
         stated — the part that makes a threshold checkable. LEAVE EMPTY if you
         cannot point at a location you are sure of.>

mechanism: <what happens, and why it helps. The finding, not the implementation.>
trigger: <the condition under which it applies -> becomes the precondition port>
derivation: <how that becomes a rule for THIS robot and THESE sensors. Numbers
             belong here, with their units, and so does the reasoning that got
             you to them.>

prediction:
  statement: <the falsifiable claim, in words>
  metric: <what gets better>
  baseline: <goal_seeker or reactive_avoid>
  min_effect: <a number: the smallest effect that would count as support>
  cost_metric: <the metric this mechanism is expected to make WORSE>

confidence: <high | medium | low>
```

### `prediction.metric` — the closed list

The metric must be one the scorer actually computes, and one a **controller can
move**. These and no others:

| metric | better |
|---|---|
| `goal_reached` | higher (a rate over seeds) |
| `spl` | higher (path efficiency) |
| `min_clearance` | higher (closest approach to anything, metres) |
| `collisions`, `near_misses` | lower |
| `stuck_events`, `time_stuck`, `recovery_time` | lower |
| `time_to_goal`, `path_length` | lower |

`localisation_failures`, `optimal_distance`, `scenario` and `seed` are **not
available**: no controller can move them, so a prediction naming one is not
falsifiable about the node and the card is rejected at load.

`cost_metric` is the honest counterpart — the metric this mechanism is expected
to make worse. A mechanism that buys clearance with time should say so. It may
be empty only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs nothing, and you
should be suspicious of that belief.

### `confidence` — criteria about the SOURCE, not about how sure you feel

- **high** — the mechanism *and* its quantitative form are stated explicitly in
  a source you can point at; the span points at the equation, threshold or
  exponent itself.
- **medium** — the mechanism is stated explicitly somewhere, but the
  quantitative form is adapted: different units, a different body scale, a
  different sensor. The number is yours; the mechanism is not.
- **low** — the mechanism is qualitative and the derivation is entirely yours.
  Still usable, but it is your claim, and the card must not read otherwise.

## Rules

- **One mechanism.** A card describing two is two cards. This is not a style
  rule: the unit scenario that decides admissibility has to isolate one claimed
  effect, and it cannot isolate two.
- **No coupling to a specific scenario.** The leaf will run on worlds nobody has
  seen. The card may not name a room, a coordinate, a doorway or a map.
- **Do not invent a `span`.** An empty span is a result and costs nothing. A
  section number reconstructed from the shape of such papers is a fabrication,
  it will be checked against the document, and it is the single failure this
  pipeline exists to detect.
- **Do not invent numbers.** If a source states a threshold, an exponent or a
  closed form, give it and say where. If it does not, derive one, say the
  derivation is yours, and set `confidence: low`.

## What to return

One fenced ```yaml block containing exactly one card, and nothing else that
looks like YAML. Prose outside the fence — including, if it applies, an honest
statement of what you did not know.

response.text:
```yaml
id: shape_anchored_goal_address
node_name: ReanchorGoalToVisibleShape

source:
  citation: >
    Cheng, K. (1986). A purely geometric module in the rat's spatial
    representation. Cognition, 23, 149-178.
  span: >
    Experiment 1B, Discussion, p. 161 ("the retention and use of both featural
    and inertial information are subsidiary to the use of the geometric
    relations between the target and the shape of the environment");
    General Discussion, p. 171 ("the rat must have recorded the metric relations
    of distances and angles between target and shape, and kept track of
    left-right relations, or sense. Metric relations and sense together are
    known as displacement properties"); Table 1, p. 158 (Exp. 1A: 47% correct
    digs vs 31% rotational errors, average over three rats).

mechanism: >
  A place is specified as an address on a metric frame built from the
  arrangement of surfaces as surfaces - the shape of the environment - and that
  address is couched in displacement properties: the metric distances and angles
  from the target to those surfaces, plus sense (which surface is to the left and
  which to the right). Cheng shows this frame outranks the two obvious
  alternatives. It outranks featural identity: in Experiment 3 a diagonal
  transposition, which scrambles the distances, angles and handedness of the
  feature arrangement but leaves the target's relations to the surfaces intact,
  produced no decrement in any rat, whereas an affine transformation or a
  reflection, which leaves the local feature on the target but moves the target
  to a geometrically different corner, produced a significant decrement in every
  rat (p < .05, .01, .001). And it outranks dead reckoning: rats kept a
  vestibular record of how far the box had been rotated during the delay, yet
  "the retention and use of both featural and inertial information are
  subsidiary to the use of the geometric relations between the target and the
  shape of the environment" (p. 161) - when the two disagreed the rats went to
  the geometrically correct place. This helps because the surface arrangement is
  re-measured directly at recall time, so an address expressed in it does not
  accumulate the error that an address expressed in an integrated-motion frame
  does. Its one failure mode is the price of the same property: when the shape
  admits two congruences with itself, the address names two places, and the
  animal takes the wrong one about as often as the right one (47% correct vs 31%
  rotational, Table 1).
trigger: >
  The goal position is disclosed, the belief about our own pose is no longer
  trustworthy, and enough surface is currently visible to define a metric frame
  whose sense is decidable. Concretely: goal is not None, pose_error_estimate
  exceeds the trust threshold, a shape frame was latched earlier while the belief
  was still trustworthy, and the currently visible surface arrangement is still
  recognisably the one that was latched. If any of these fails - goal
  undisclosed, belief still good, too few returns, shape near-symmetric so sense
  is undecidable, or the visible arrangement has changed - the leaf returns
  FAILURE and the tree falls through to steering by pose_estimate.

derivation: >
  Mapping. Cheng's "arrangement of surfaces as surfaces" becomes the set of
  finite lidar returns: 181 beams, anything with r < range_max is a surface
  point, inf is no surface. His "inertial/vestibular record" becomes
  pose_estimate, which is the drifting integrated-motion belief, with
  pose_error_estimate as the robot's own confession of how far it has drifted.
  His "featural information" (brightness, texture, odour of a panel) has no
  counterpart on a planar lidar and is dropped - this card claims nothing about
  features. The paper's target-to-shape address becomes the goal's coordinates
  in a frame computed from the scan. All of this mapping is mine; Cheng never
  discusses range sensors, partial visibility or a moving observer.

  Building the frame (each control step). Take the finite returns and convert to
  robot-frame points p_i = (r_i*cos(theta_i), r_i*sin(theta_i)) using
  range_angles. Require N >= 40 of the 181 beams finite, else abstain - fewer
  than that is not an arrangement of surfaces, it is a corridor mouth. Centroid
  c = mean(p_i). Second-moment matrix M = sum (p_i - c)(p_i - c)^T / N, with
  eigenvalues lam1 >= lam2 and unit eigenvectors. Let e1 be the major
  eigenvector and set e2 = rot90(e1) so the pair is always right-handed; that
  right-handedness is how sense is carried, which Cheng (p. 171) says the rat
  carries too, and which is why the frame must never be built by an operation
  that is blind to reflection.

  Resolving the rotational ambiguity. e1 is defined only up to sign, and the two
  signs are exactly Cheng's target and its rotational equivalent. Break the tie
  with a statistic that a 180-degree-symmetric shape cannot supply: the third
  moment along the axis, m3 = sum ((p_i - c).e1)^3 / N. Choose the sign of e1
  that makes m3 >= 0. If the normalised skew |m3| / lam1^1.5 < 0.05, the visible
  shape is too close to 180-degree symmetric for sense to be decided, and the
  leaf abstains rather than committing. The rat commits and is wrong 31 times in
  100 (Table 1, p. 158); a robot that abstains keeps the drifting belief, which
  is bad, instead of a confidently mirrored address, which is worse. The 40-beam
  minimum and the 0.05 skew threshold are mine; the paper states no threshold of
  either kind.

  Latching the address. While pose_error_estimate <= 0.30 m the belief is
  treated as trustworthy. On any such step, express the goal offset in the shape
  frame: d = R(-yaw) * (goal - (x,y)) from pose_estimate, then u = (d - c).e1,
  v = (d - c).e2. Store (u, v) together with a shape signature (lam1, lam2, N).
  The 0.30 m trust threshold is mine, chosen as roughly half the Go2's body
  length, on the reasoning that a belief wrong by less than half a body is not
  yet what is making the robot miss.

  Using the address. Once pose_error_estimate > 0.30 m, recompute c, e1, e2 and
  the signature from the live scan. Accept the frame only if
  |lam1/lam1_latched - 1| <= 0.25 and |lam2/lam2_latched - 1| <= 0.25 - the same
  arrangement of surfaces, seen from somewhere else, not a different room. Then
  reconstruct the goal in the robot frame as g = c + u*e1 + v*e2 and steer to
  that instead of to the pose-derived offset. Twist: psi = atan2(g_y, g_x),
  wz = clip(2.0*psi, -1.0, 1.0), vx = 0.8*cos(psi) if |psi| <= 1.0 rad else 0.0,
  vy = 0.0. The 0.25 signature tolerance and the steering gains are mine. When
  the signature test fails, the leaf abstains and re-latches at the next step
  where pose_error_estimate <= 0.30 m.

  Where the mapping breaks, plainly. Cheng's box is fully visible from every
  point inside it, so his metric frame is global and permanent. A 6 m lidar in an
  indoor space sees one room's worth of surface, so this frame is local and
  temporary: it corrects drift accumulated since the latch, while the same
  surfaces stay in view, and it cannot correct drift accumulated before the
  latch or survive a doorway. That limitation is a property of the sensor, not
  of the paper, and it is the main reason this card's confidence is not high.

prediction:
  statement: >
    On runs where pose_estimate drifts, steering the final approach by the goal's
    address in the shape frame rather than by the pose belief raises the fraction
    of episodes that reach the goal, because the address is re-measured against
    visible surfaces every step instead of inheriting accumulated belief error.
  metric: goal_reached
  baseline: goal_seeker
  min_effect: 0.10
  cost_metric: path_length

confidence: medium
```

Two things I could not settle from the document. Cheng never states a tolerance for "the same metric frame" or a test for when a shape is too symmetric to be usable — he documents the rotational error rather than a rule for avoiding it — so the 0.05 skew threshold, the 0.25 signature tolerance, the 40-beam floor and the 0.30 m trust threshold are all mine and none of them should be attributed to him. The one number in the paper that looks like a place tolerance, the 15 cm scoring radius covering 10% of the 120x60 cm floor (Exp. 1A, Dependent measure/Results, pp. 156-157), is the experimenter's scoring criterion, not a measured property of the rat, so I did not carry it across as a capture radius.

I also did not carry across the featural half of the paper at all. Cheng's second result — that features are checked only near the geometrically specified address, not as an overall arrangement — is a real and separable mechanism, but a planar lidar returns range and nothing else, so there is no featural channel here to gate. If the platform ever gains one (a camera, a floor-texture sensor), that is a second card, not an extension of this one.
